title: Put the nursery’s requirements at the centre of the brief
focus: Share the age groups, meal schedule, service setting and the nursery’s food policies before discussing a menu. Portion sizes, textures, ingredient requirements and the handover process need specific review with the responsible staff. Allergy information and any specialist needs must be assessed through the nursery’s established procedures. The proposed provider should supply relevant information for the organisation’s approval process. No service should be assumed suitable until the menu, facilities and required arrangements have been confirmed.

sections.title: Connect meal planning to the nursery routine
paragraphs: Begin with the room groups, ages and daily routine at the centre. Record when each group eats, who assists at the table and where meals are received. The catering proposal should fit the nursery schedule, including rest periods and collection times, so food service becomes a predictable part of the day.

Explain how families enrol for meals and how attendance changes reach the kitchen. If some children bring food from home, the nursery decides the rules for that arrangement. A clear ordering record helps staff distinguish what has been requested and reduces confusion when a child is absent or a family changes its plan.

Agree who approves the menu cycle and who reviews preparation requirements for each age group. The nursery should supply its relevant policies and identify any individual needs requiring professional input. The proposed culinary partner can then assess the brief and record what can be accommodated before the programme is confirmed.

sections.title: Make individual meal requirements easy to follow
paragraphs: Dietary information should move through one agreed nursery contact. Keep the current requirements, approved ingredients and meal identification consistent across the order and handover. Families need a clear way to report changes to the nursery, while the kitchen needs enough notice to assess whether the change can be accommodated.

A nut restriction or other allergy policy must be discussed in precise terms. Ingredient choices, supply information and preparation conditions all matter. Do not infer that a dish is suitable solely from its name or appearance. The provider must assess the actual request, and the nursery confirms the arrangements it requires before service starts.

Preparation and portions also need to reflect the children receiving the meals. The nursery team reviews age-group requirements and any individual instructions, with specialist input where appropriate. Sample dishes are useful for discussion, but the final menu and handling arrangements should be approved for the centre rather than copied from an adult menu.

sections.title: Agree a calm delivery and handover
paragraphs: Set a delivery window that leaves time for the nursery team to receive and check the order before children sit down. Name the receiving contact and a backup, explain access to the building and confirm where meals will be handed over. The team should know whom to contact if anything differs from the confirmed order.

The proposal records the handling information, required checks and any equipment involved. Agree the responsibilities for serving, clearing and returning reusable items. If the centre has several rooms, decide how meals are distributed internally and how individual requirements remain identifiable through that handover.

Review the introduction period with the people who serve the children each day. Feedback on portions, menu acceptance, packaging and timing can reveal useful adjustments. Confirm changes with management and the culinary partner, then update the written plan so the next service reflects the agreed decisions.
